“Information received since the September meeting indicates continued labor-market strength and economic activity rising at a strong rate, with inflation near 2 percent and longer-term inflation expectations little changed. This configuration is consistent with the expectations-augmented Phillips curve of Friedman and Phelps, which implies no lasting unemployment–inflation trade-off once expectations are anchored, and with New Keynesian models (Galí and Gertler 1999; Woodford 2003; Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans 2005) in which forward-looking inflation expectations play a central role. The Committee’s choice to hold the federal funds rate at 2 to 2-1/4 percent while signaling further gradual increases, and to continue balance-sheet normalization, aligns with the literature that expected inflation influences nominal interest rates and that credibility helps prevent self-fulfilling ‘inflation scares’ (Cagan 1956; Svensson). With inflation near target, estimated welfare costs of inflation (e.g., Feldstein) remain relatively low, though the noted moderation in business fixed investment tempers the otherwise strong tone.”
